author: hudson-taylor
fields.title: A Retrospect (For Teens)
fields.description: Hudson Taylor was a real teenager who doubted, feared, and worried about money — then staked his whole life on a God he decided to actually test. This teen edition retells the true story behind the China Inland Mission: the last coin given away, the deadly needle-prick, the storm off the rocks, a night robbed on temple steps, and one prayer written in a Bible’s margin.

qa.question: Who was Hudson Taylor?
qa.answer: He was a young Englishman who, in the 1850s, gave up an ordinary career to carry the good news of Jesus into inland China, trusting God to supply everything he needed. He later founded the China Inland Mission.

qa.question: What does “the finished work of Christ” mean?
qa.answer: It means Jesus’ death paid for sin completely, so there is nothing left for you to earn or add. Taylor was converted the moment he understood he only had to receive it, not achieve it.

qa.question: Why did Taylor keep letting himself run out of money on purpose?
qa.answer: Before sailing to a country where he would have no one to ask but God, he wanted to find out whether his faith could actually move things through prayer alone. He practised trusting God for small needs so he could trust him for large ones.

qa.question: What happened the night he gave away his last half-crown?
qa.answer: He handed his only coin to a starving family, keeping nothing back for himself. The next morning an unsigned envelope arrived containing ten shillings — four times what he had given away.

qa.question: Was Taylor ever actually afraid?
qa.answer: Yes — of drowning in a storm off the Welsh rocks, of dying from an infected finger, and of being robbed alone on temple steps at night. He was honest that his own faith often failed, and that God stayed faithful anyway.

qa.question: What was the prayer he wrote in the margin of his Bible?
qa.answer: On a beach at Brighton in 1865 he asked God for twenty-four fellow workers for inland China and wrote the request in the margin of the Bible he had with him. That prayer became the beginning of the China Inland Mission.

qa.question: Why did he dress in Chinese clothing?
qa.answer: He wanted people to hear the message instead of being distracted by a foreigner, so he gave up his own comfort and pride and dressed like those he served. His friend William Burns was so struck by the difference it made that he did the same.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from Taylor’s story?
qa.answer: That God can be tested and trusted with real, specific needs — money, fear, direction — and that obeying him usually costs something before it proves worth it. Taylor began as a doubting teenager, not a finished saint.

fields.title: It Is Finished
fields.body_html:
“When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, ‘It is finished,’ and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.” — John 19:30 (ESV)

Before Hudson Taylor believed anything, he doubted almost everything. He had grown up in a Christian home, watched his parents pray, and heard the Bible read — and it had left him cold. He had tried, more than once, to make himself into a Christian by sheer effort, failed every time, and quietly concluded that salvation simply was not for someone like him. So he went looking for a way out. He fell in with people who held sceptical, unbelieving views, and he took them up gladly, because if the Bible was not true, then the future it warned about was not true either.

But even as a doubter, Taylor was honest, and his honesty is worth copying. He noticed that the loudest argument against Christianity came from Christians themselves — people who claimed to believe the Bible while living exactly as they would have lived if it were fiction. And he made a private vow: if he ever did claim to believe this book, he would actually put it to the test. He would live by it, and if it failed him, he would throw it out entirely. Hold on to that. He carried that willingness to test God into the rest of his life.

The turning point came on an ordinary afternoon when he was about fifteen. His mother was away, he had nothing to do, and he pulled a Gospel booklet out of a basket purely to kill time. He fully intended to read the interesting story at the front and skip the sermon at the end. But one phrase snagged him: the finished work of Christ. Why finished, he wondered? And the words of Jesus from the cross rose up in his mind — “It is finished.” If the whole debt for sin had already been paid, in full, by someone else, then what was left for Hudson to do? Nothing. Nothing but kneel down and accept it.

That was it. Alone in a quiet warehouse, he gave his life to Jesus — not because he had finally become good enough, but because he saw that he never had to be.

Here is why this matters for you, especially if you are the doubting type. Taylor was not argued into faith and he was not scared into it. He was floored by one idea: that the most important work in the universe was already done, and done by someone other than him. Most people spend their lives trying to earn their way to being okay — okay with their parents, okay with their friends, okay with themselves, okay with God. “It is finished” cuts straight through that. Jesus did not say “It is started” or “Now it is your turn.” He said it is finished. You do not add to a completed payment. You receive it.

And notice this: your doubts are not disqualifying. Taylor’s scepticism did not have to be beaten out of him before God could reach him. In fact his refusal to fake belief was the very thing that kept him honest enough to be caught by the truth when it came. God is not afraid of your hard questions. He is only shut out by the pretending — either pretending to believe when you do not, or pretending you are fine when you are not.

One thing to do today: stop trying to earn what has already been paid for. Take five minutes alone, and instead of promising God you will try harder, tell him the truth about where you actually stand — your real doubts, your real state — and then say plainly that you accept the finished work of Christ as a gift, not a wage. Test it. Taylor did, and he never got to the end of it.

fields.title: The Locked Room
fields.body_html:
“And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart.” — Luke 18:1 (ESV)

On the very afternoon Hudson Taylor sat reading that booklet, his mother was seventy or eighty miles away, and she could not stop thinking about him. She got up from lunch with what she later called an intense longing for her son’s conversion, and she realised that being away from home, with no chores and no interruptions, had handed her a rare stretch of free hours. So she went to her room, turned the key in the lock, and made herself a promise: she would not leave that spot until God answered.

Hour after hour she prayed for him. And then something strange happened. At a certain point she found she could not keep asking — instead she was moved to start thanking God, because she was somehow sure the thing was already done. Her son was converted. She did not know how she knew; she just praised God for it and got up.

When she came home a fortnight later, Hudson ran to meet her at the door, bursting to tell her his news. Before he could get it out, she put her arms around him and said, “I know, my boy. I have been rejoicing for a fortnight in the glad tidings you have to tell me.” He was baffled — he had told only his sister, and sworn her to secrecy. His mother assured him she had heard it from no human being at all, and told him about the locked room.

There was more. Some time later Hudson picked up a little pocket-book he thought was his own, opened it, and found it was his sister Amelia’s diary. One entry stopped him: she had resolved to pray for her brother’s conversion every single day until God answered. He worked out the date. It was exactly one month before the afternoon he knelt down in the warehouse.

Now, be careful how you read this. The point is not that Taylor’s mother forced God’s hand by staying in a room, as if prayer were a machine where enough hours in one end produces a result out the other. If you have ever prayed hard for someone and watched nothing change, you know that is not how it works, and pretending otherwise only breaks your heart. What this story shows is something quieter and tougher: two people who kept praying for one specific person, over weeks and months, without any visible sign that it was doing a thing — and did not give up.

That is exactly what Jesus’ words in Luke are about. He did not say “pray until you feel like stopping.” He said pray “and do not lose heart.” The temptation is never really to quit praying; it is to quietly conclude it is pointless and drift off. Taylor’s mother refused to drift. His sister wrote it down and held herself to it daily. Neither of them could see the warehouse, or the booklet, or the phrase that would undo him. They just kept asking.

If you are a Christian, there is almost certainly a name that belongs to you the way Hudson’s belonged to his mother — a friend, a sibling, a parent who wants nothing to do with God. You cannot argue them into the kingdom, you cannot manufacture the moment truth lands, and you will usually get zero feedback. What you can do is refuse to lose heart.

One thing to do this week: pick one person you long to see come to God, and write their name down somewhere you will actually see it — the back of your journal, a note on your phone. Then commit to praying for them by name once a day for a set stretch of time, whether or not anything appears to happen. Taylor was living proof that the person being prayed for often has no idea it is going on.

fields.title: The Last Half-Crown
fields.body_html:
“Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.” — Proverbs 19:17 (ESV)

Hudson Taylor was training to be a doctor in Hull, and he was also, on purpose, training his faith. He had decided that before he ever sailed for China — where he would have no one on earth to ask for money — he needed to learn to depend on God alone. So he lived on almost nothing, gave away as much as he could, and tried to trust God for the rest.

One Saturday night that experiment got real. After settling his accounts he was left with a single coin — one half-crown — and nothing else in the world. He was not worried yet; Sunday was a happy day of preaching in the poorest lodging-houses in town. But late that night, near ten o’clock, a poor man asked him to come and pray with his dying wife. On the way Taylor asked why he had not fetched the priest. The man had tried; the priest wanted eighteenpence to come, and the family was starving.

And there it was. Taylor had exactly one coin, and it was a half-crown — two shillings and sixpence — that could not be broken. Climbing the filthy stairs, he found a scene that gutted him: half-starved children with sunken cheeks, and a mother lying on a wretched bed with a baby barely a day and a half old, too weak even to cry properly. Taylor started to tell them about a kind and loving Father in heaven — and a voice inside him said, You hypocrite. You are telling these people to trust a Father you will not trust yourself, because you are clutching a half-crown.

He was completely honest, years later, about what was really going on. “I could trust God plus one-and-sixpence,” he wrote, “but I was not yet prepared to trust him only.” If he had had change — a florin and a sixpence — he would gladly have given part and kept the rest. It was giving everything he could not face. Then the father said, “If you can help us, for God’s sake do.” And a line of Scripture flashed into his mind: give to the one who asks. He pulled out the coin, handed it over, and told them that in giving it he was giving them all he had — and that what he had been saying was true: God really is a Father, and can be trusted. Instantly the joy came flooding back.

He walked home to a supper of watery porridge, singing in the empty streets, with a pocket as light as his heart. The next morning, before the porridge was even finished, the post arrived — unusual for a Monday. Inside a blank sheet of paper, folded in a pair of gloves, was half a sovereign: ten shillings. Four times what he had given away, back in twelve hours.

Do not misread this as a formula: give God money and he pays you back with interest, guaranteed, by breakfast. That is not the lesson, and treating God like an investment app will wreck your faith the first time the envelope does not come. Look instead at what Taylor was actually fighting. He had a exact number in his head — one-and-sixpence — that marked the border of his trust. Right up to that line he would obey. Past it, he wanted a safety margin. And he saw, with painful clarity, that “God plus a backup plan” is not really trusting God at all.

You have that line too. It is the amount of money, or comfort, or control you are willing to risk for God — right up to the point where it stops feeling safe. The whole of the Christian life happens on the other side of that line.

One thing to do this week: find your “one-and-sixpence” — the specific thing you will give, share, or risk only if you get to keep a safety margin — and give past it, once, on purpose. Not recklessly, but really. You cannot find out God is trustworthy while you are still holding a backup.

fields.title: The Salary Nobody Mentioned
fields.body_html:
“And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.” — Philippians 4:19 (ESV)

Taylor kept setting himself deliberate tests, and one of them sounds almost stubborn. His employer, a kind and busy doctor, had asked Taylor to simply remind him whenever his salary fell due. Fair enough. But Taylor decided he would not remind him. Instead he would pray — and ask God to bring it to the doctor’s mind. His reasoning was blunt: “When I get out to China, I shall have no claim on anyone for anything; my only claim will be on God. How important, therefore, to learn before leaving England to move man, through God, by prayer alone.”

So the salary came due, and Taylor said nothing, and prayed. Days passed. The doctor forgot. Eventually Taylor was down to that famous single half-crown, then, after the ten shillings arrived, back down to almost nothing again — with rent owed to his landlady, a poor Christian woman who was counting on it. Now the test had a second person caught in it. Should he speak up for her sake? He gave nearly two whole days to wrestling in prayer, and as far as he could tell, the answer was: wait.

Late one Saturday afternoon the doctor, relaxing after work, suddenly said, “By the bye, Taylor, is not your salary due again?” Taylor’s heart leapt — God had done it, reminded him with no hint from Taylor at all. He kept his voice steady and said yes, it was overdue. And then the doctor said the worst possible thing: “Oh, I am so sorry — only this afternoon I sent all my money to the bank. I wish I had thought of it sooner.” The relief collapsed. Taylor had to grab a boiling pan as an excuse to bolt from the room before his face gave him away.

He went home that night with nothing, still trusting, hoping God might act by Monday. But around ten o’clock the doctor came into the surgery, laughing to himself. One of his richest patients had just turned up — after ten at night — to pay his doctor’s bill in cash. Who does that? The man could have posted a cheque any day; instead he had felt he could not rest until he came round at that ridiculous hour and settled it. The doctor pocketed the notes, then turned back and said, “By the way, Taylor, you might as well take these; I have no change, but I can give you the balance next week.”

Here is the part that is easy to skate past: God did not answer the way Taylor expected. He expected the doctor to remember and pay — and the doctor did remember, and could not pay. If Taylor had been watching only for his one imagined solution, he would have gone to bed that Saturday convinced God had failed him. The reminder and the money came through two completely different people, at two different moments, in an order that made no sense until it was over.

You will do this constantly. You will pray for something and decide, without noticing, exactly how God is allowed to answer — this person apologises, that opportunity opens, the money comes from here. And when your specific script does not play out, it feels like a no. Taylor’s Saturday is a warning against that. The need was real, the answer was coming, and it looked like failure right up until the last hour.

God promises to supply your need. He does not promise to supply it through the door you are staring at.

One thing to do: take something you have been praying about, and notice — honestly — the exact outcome you have secretly decided would count as God answering. Write it down. Then deliberately hand him permission to answer some other way, and start watching the doors you were not looking at. Taylor’s help walked in at ten at night, from a direction he never considered.

fields.title: “You Are a Dead Man”
fields.body_html:
“I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD.” — Psalm 118:17 (ESV)

Taylor had moved to London to finish his medical training, living on brown bread, water, and a few apples, walking eight or nine miles a day to save money. One evening, sewing together sheets of paper to take lecture notes, he pricked the first finger of his right hand with the needle. It was nothing. He forgot about it within moments.

The next day at the hospital he was dissecting a body — and not just any body. This one had died of a fever so dangerous that everyone working on it did so with extreme care, knowing the smallest scratch could be fatal. Before the morning was over Taylor felt strangely exhausted, then violently sick, then unable to hold his pencil. By afternoon his whole right arm and side were in severe pain. He described his symptoms to the demonstrator, a skilled surgeon, who understood at once: Taylor had a cut, and this was a case of malignant fever. Taylor insisted he had no cut — then remembered the needle-prick from the night before. The surgeon examined his hand, agreed that was almost certainly the way the poison had entered, and told him plainly to get a cab home and put his affairs in order. “For,” he said, “you are a dead man.”

Taylor’s first reaction was grief — not fear of death, but sorrow that he would never make it to China. And then, almost immediately, came a settled conviction: Unless I am greatly mistaken, I have work to do in China, and shall not die. He even told the sceptical surgeon so, and used the moment to speak to him about the joy of possibly soon being with his Master. The surgeon just told him to hurry home before he became incapable of sorting out his affairs.

Taylor could not afford a cab. Growing weaker, he walked and took omnibuses as far as he could, got home in agony, lanced the finger himself to try to release the poison, and fainted. An uncle sent for a surgeon, who said Taylor might pull through only because he had been living so soberly — bread and water, as it happened, was the best possible preparation. He ordered port wine and chops Taylor had no money to buy; the uncle quietly paid for them. Weeks of suffering followed. And then Taylor learned that two other men who had received dissection wounds at the same time had both died. He had lived.

Be careful what you take from this. He believed there was something God still meant him to do, and that belief did not make him reckless; it made him calm.

fields.title: Within a Stone’s Throw
fields.body_html:
“He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed.” — Psalm 107:29 (ESV)

On the 19th of September 1853, Taylor finally sailed for China aboard the Dumfries. His mother had come to see him off, smoothed the little bed in his cabin with her own hands, prayed with him one last time, and gone ashore. As the ship passed through the dock gates and the real parting began, Taylor heard a cry of anguish torn out of her. He said later he never understood the words “God so loved the world” until that moment — watching what love costs when you let go of someone for the sake of others.

The voyage nearly ended almost before it began. They had barely left port when a violent gale caught them, and for twelve days they were flung back and forth in the Irish Channel, unable to reach open sea. The storm kept building. By Sunday night the ship was being driven straight toward the rocks of Carnarvon Bay, each turn bringing them closer, until they were within a stone’s throw of the shore. The Christian captain turned to the young missionary and said the thing everyone was thinking: “We cannot live half an hour now. What of your call to labour for the Lord in China?”

It is a brutal question — your whole faith, your whole future, tested against a wall of rock in the dark. And Taylor’s answer was not bravado. He said he would not, for anything, be in any other position; that he still expected to reach China, but that if not, at least the Master would say it was well that he had died trying to obey. A few minutes later, after the ship was turned, the captain came back to the compass and said, “The wind has freed two points; we shall be able to beat out of the bay.” And they did. The ship was strained and damaged, but it lived.

Now here is the honest, uncomfortable part Taylor insisted on telling — and it is the reason this chapter is not just an adventure story. Before the voyage, to please his mother, he had bought a swimming-belt. But he had talked himself into a strange idea: that he could not really trust God while he owned a life-saving device. So on that terrible night, once all hope seemed gone, he gave the belt away — and then, oddly, gathered up some light objects likely to float, without noticing the contradiction. Later, studying the Bible carefully, he decided the whole thing had been a mistake. Real faith does not mean throwing away the help God provides. For years afterward he carried a swimming-belt with no trouble at all.

Read that twice, because a lot of sincere young Christians get this exactly wrong. Taylor thought spirituality meant refusing the ordinary means of safety — as if trusting God and using a life-belt were rivals. They are not. Using the means God gives is not a failure of faith; neglecting them is not a proof of it. The same God who calms the storm is the God who invented the swimming-belt.

You will meet a version of this. It shows up as the idea that “really trusting God” means not studying for the exam, not seeing the doctor, not making a plan — just praying and leaving it. That is not faith; it is a superstition that dresses up as faith and then blames God when it fails. Taylor learned the difference the hard way, in the dark, off the rocks. Trust God completely and use everything he has put in your hand. The two were never enemies.

One thing to do: find the place where you have been treating faith and effort as opposites — the subject you are “trusting God” with instead of preparing for, the problem you are praying about instead of acting on — and this week do both at once. Pray hard, and pick up the swimming-belt. Taylor eventually saw there was never any conflict.

fields.title: Pray for a Wind
fields.body_html:
“Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven.” — Matthew 18:19 (ESV)

The same long voyage that nearly ended on the rocks nearly ended a second time — this time not from too much wind, but from none. As the Dumfries came near the north coast of New Guinea, the wind died completely and a strong current took over, dragging the ship steadily toward a line of hidden reefs. The crew put out the long-boat and rowed with everything they had, trying to pull the ship’s head around. It did not work. They drifted closer. On the shore, Taylor could see people running about on the sand, lighting fires — and the captain’s reference book warned that these islanders were cannibals. It was, as Taylor dryly put it, “not a little alarming.”

After a while the captain and Taylor stood on deck in silence. Finally the captain said, “Well, we have done everything that can be done; we can only await the result.” And Taylor answered, “No, there is one thing we have not done yet.” “What is it?” “Four of us on board are Christians. Let us each go to our own cabin and agree together in prayer for a breeze. God can send it now as easily as at sunset.”

The captain agreed. Taylor found the other two believers — the Swedish carpenter and the ship’s steward — and all four went to pray. Taylor had barely started when he felt so certain the request was granted that he could not keep asking, and he went straight back up on deck. The first officer, a hard, godless man, was on watch. Taylor asked him to let down the corners of the mainsail, which had been drawn up to stop it flapping uselessly. “What would be the good of that?” the man sneered. Taylor told him they had asked God for wind, it was coming immediately, and the reef was too close to lose a minute. The officer swore he would rather see a wind than hear about one. But as he spoke, Taylor watched his eyes drift upward — and there, at the very top of the mast, the corner of the highest sail had begun to tremble. “Don’t you see the wind is coming? Look at the royal!” The officer dismissed it as a stray puff. “Cat’s-paw or not,” Taylor shouted, “let down the mainsail and let us have the benefit!”

He did. Within minutes the breeze filled the canvas, the ship was cutting through the water at six or seven knots, and the reef — and the crowd waiting on the beach — fell safely behind them.

Notice how specific this prayer was. Not “God, keep us safe” in general, but “send a wind, now, from this direction, before that reef.” Taylor asked for exactly what the situation needed, and he asked with others, in agreement, which is the very thing Jesus points to in Matthew 18. There is something about praying a concrete request alongside other believers that God honours again and again in Scripture.

A lot of prayer stays deliberately vague, and if you are honest you know why: a vague prayer can never obviously go unanswered. “Bless everyone, be with me today” can never fail — but it also never really tests anything, and it never grows your faith, because you can never point to the moment God moved. Taylor prayed prayers that could visibly succeed or visibly fail, and precisely because of that, he spent his life collecting evidence that God answers.

That takes nerve. A specific prayer is a risk. It puts God’s faithfulness where you can actually see it, which means it also puts your disappointment where you can actually feel it. But it is the only kind of praying that ever taught anyone what God can do.

One thing to do this week: turn one of your vague prayers into a specific one, and if you can, ask a Christian friend to agree with you on it. Not “help me with school,” but the actual thing — the conversation, the exact need, the real fear. Then watch. Taylor built a whole life on prayers concrete enough to be answered in front of witnesses.

fields.title: Becoming One of Them
fields.body_html:
“To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.” — 1 Corinthians 9:22 (ESV)

When Taylor first reached China he did what nearly every foreigner did: he stayed a foreigner. He wore his English clothes, kept his English haircut, and looked exactly like what he was — an outsider from the other side of the world. And the effect was constant. In some places he and his companions were followed through the streets by shouts of “foreign devil,” “foreign dog,” “foreign pig.” Everywhere he went, the clothes announced him before he could open his mouth, and people reacted to the strange Englishman instead of listening to what he had come to say.

On the advice of an experienced older missionary, Taylor made a decision most of his countrymen thought was undignified, even embarrassing: he adopted Chinese dress. He put on the long gown, and he wore his hair in the style of the people around him. To a proud young Englishman of the 1850s, this felt like a genuine loss of status — deliberately making himself look like the people others sneered at.

But the results were impossible to argue with, and the clearest proof came through his friend William Burns, an older and more experienced preacher whom Taylor deeply admired. The two of them travelled and preached together, Burns still in his English clothes, Taylor now in Chinese dress. And Burns could not help noticing the difference. Taylor, in local dress, drew quiet, attentive listeners; he was invited into people’s homes. Burns, in his foreign suit, drew crowds of rude boys and gawkers, and was politely never invited anywhere, because hosting a foreigner meant hosting the mob that trailed him. After some weeks of watching this, Burns — the senior man — humbled himself and adopted Chinese dress too, and found the same doors opening.

Think about what Taylor actually gave up here. Not comfort, mainly — pride. He surrendered the right to be recognised, respected, and treated as the important visitor he technically was. He made himself look ordinary, even lowly, to people who already looked down on his kind, so that nothing about his appearance would get in the way of the one thing he came to give them. He decided the message mattered more than his image.

That instinct runs dead against everything you are trained to want. Almost every message aimed at you says the opposite: stand out, build your brand, curate your look, protect your image, make sure people see how interesting and different you are. Taylor did the reverse on purpose. He worked out that his own distinctiveness — the very thing that made him noticeable — was the thing standing between people and Jesus, so he laid it down.

Paul said the same about himself: he became whatever he needed to become to win people, sacrificing his own preferences and status “that by all means I might save some.” This is not about being fake or having no convictions — Taylor’s convictions never bent an inch. It is about being willing to be less impressive, less noticed, less catered-to, for the sake of someone else actually hearing you.

You will feel this most sharply with people who are different from you — a new kid nobody talks to, someone from another background, someone the group has quietly decided is beneath them. Loving them almost always costs you a little standing. You have to step down from wherever you rank to meet them where they are, and people will notice you did it, and some will think less of you for it. Taylor thought that was a bargain.

One thing to do: find the person or group you have been keeping at arm’s length partly to protect your own image, and close the distance in a way that costs you something visible — sit with them, stand with them, be seen with them. Taylor changed his entire appearance so that nothing about him would keep people from Jesus. Start with something a good deal smaller than that.

fields.title: The Temple Steps
fields.body_html:
“And Jesus said to him, ‘Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.’” — Matthew 8:20 (ESV)

Taylor was travelling overland to the city of Ningpo, carrying nearly everything he owned in China — his watch, surgical instruments, books, bedding — with a hired servant looking after the luggage. Partway through the journey, the two got separated. Taylor walked ahead, expecting the servant to follow with the coolies carrying the bags. The servant never came. As the day wore on, Taylor slowly realised the truth: the man had taken all his belongings and vanished toward another city. Taylor was alone, far from any friend, with almost no money and nothing but the clothes he stood in.

Night fell in the city of Hai-ning, and he could not find anywhere to sleep. He tried inn after inn; some turned him away, others promised him a bed and then, frightened off by an official who kept following him, sent him back into the street. One young man led him around for hours, apparently to help, then abandoned him between one and two in the morning to fend for himself. Exhausted, blistered, and cold, Taylor found himself in front of a closed temple, lay down on the stone steps, and put his small store of money under his head for a pillow.

Then it got worse. A figure came creeping toward him through the dark — one of the many beggars in that region, clearly intending to rob him while he slept. Taylor did not move. He watched, and prayed, and when the man reached out and began quietly feeling for the money, Taylor spoke in a calm voice, just enough to show he was wide awake: “What do you want?” The man slipped away. But he came back, this time with a companion, and later a third, all settling near Taylor’s feet, all clearly waiting for him to fall asleep so they could take everything he had. To stay awake — and to keep them off — Taylor spent the rest of the night singing hymns, reciting Scripture aloud, and praying out loud in English, which annoyed the thieves so much that they eventually gave up and left him just before dawn.

Here is what makes this more than a scary night. On the road afterward, thinking it over, Taylor was struck by his own heart. He had been frantic about losing a few possessions — and far less troubled about the crowds of people around him who did not know Christ. He thought of Jesus, “despised and rejected,” with nowhere to lay his head, weary and hungry at a well, and he measured his own small love against that. He came away not bitter about the robbery but ashamed of how little the eternal things had gripped him compared to his luggage.

That is worth sitting with, because your instincts run the same way as his did. When you lose something — money, a phone, status, a relationship, a plan — the panic is instant and total. It swallows everything. And the things that actually last forever, including the people around you and where they stand with God, barely register by comparison. Taylor did not scold himself for feeling the loss; losing everything on cold stone steps genuinely hurts. He noticed the proportion was off: how loud the small loss was, how quiet the enormous one.

Jesus had nowhere to lay his head — by choice, for you. He gave up infinitely more than a bag of instruments, and he did it on purpose, for people who mostly did not care. When that sinks in, a stolen suitcase shrinks to roughly its real size.

One thing to do the next time you lose something: before you spiral, name honestly how much panic the loss is generating — and then ask yourself when you last felt even a fraction of that intensity about someone’s soul, including your own. You are not trying to stop caring about your stuff. You are trying, like Taylor, to get the proportions right.

It swallows everything. And the things that actually last forever, including the people around you and where they stand with God, barely register by comparison. Taylor did not scold himself for feeling the loss; losing everything on cold stone steps genuinely hurts. He noticed the proportion was off: how loud the small loss was, how quiet the enormous one. Jesus had nowhere to lay his head — by choice, for you. He gave up infinitely more than a bag of instruments, and he did it on purpose, for people who mostly did not care. When that sinks in, a stolen suitcase shrinks to roughly its real size. One thing to do the next time you lose something: before you spiral, name honestly how much panic the loss is generating — and then ask yourself when you last felt even a fraction of that intensity about someone’s soul, including your own. You are not trying to stop caring about your stuff. You are trying, like Taylor, to get the proportions right.

fields.title: The Man Who Robbed Him
fields.body_html:
“Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” — Romans 12:21 (ESV)

When the dust settled, there was no doubt about what had happened. The servant Taylor had trusted had not simply wandered off — he had deliberately stolen everything Taylor owned in China, around forty pounds’ worth of goods, a huge sum for a man living hand to mouth, and had fled with it to another city. And Taylor had a decision to make. It would not have been hard to go after the man legally. He could have set the authorities on him and had him punished.

But two things stopped him. The first was practical and a little bitter: even if the man were caught and punished, Taylor was unlikely ever to see his belongings again, so prosecution would mostly just satisfy the desire to see the thief suffer. The second thing mattered far more. This thief was a man Taylor had personally worked and prayed for — someone he wanted to see come to Christ. And Taylor had been reading, with this very man, the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus says “resist not evil” and tells his followers to answer wrong in a way the world finds baffling. Taylor decided he could not preach those words on Monday and ignore them the moment they cost him.

So he made his choice openly: the man’s soul was worth more than forty pounds of luggage. Instead of a warrant, Taylor sent the thief a letter. In it he urged the man to consider what he had done, warned him about the state of his soul, and pleaded with him to repent and put his faith in the Lord Jesus. He answered the robbery with a gospel appeal to the robber.

Taylor never records that the man wrote back or was converted; he is honest about that. What he does record is what happened at his own end. When his Christian friends in England heard how he had responded, one of them was so moved that he sent Taylor a cheque for forty pounds — the exact value of what had been stolen. And that man became a regular supporter, the first of many gifts from the same source. Taylor is careful not to present this as a reward transaction, as if forgiveness reliably refunds your losses. He simply notes that in choosing the man’s soul over his own repayment, he lost nothing in the end that mattered.

Now, be honest about how alien this is. Everything in you, when someone genuinely wrongs you — steals from you, lies about you, betrays a trust — wants them to pay. Not to be helped. Not to be prayed for. To pay. And our culture will back you all the way: they deserve it, stand up for yourself, do not let anyone walk over you. Taylor felt all of that. He specifically says it would have been easy to have the man punished. He chose the harder thing not because he was a doormat, but because he genuinely wanted something better for the man than justice — he wanted him saved.

That is what Paul means by not being overcome by evil. When someone wrongs you, there are two possible outcomes for your own heart: either their evil turns you bitter, vengeful, and hard — in which case their evil has won twice, once on you and once in you — or you refuse to let it, and you answer with a good it cannot corrupt. Taylor would not let a thief turn him into someone who cared more about repayment than about a lost man.

You do not have to pretend the wrong did not happen; Taylor never pretended. You do not have to feel warm about the person. You have to decide who you are going to become as a result of what they did.

One thing to do: think of someone who has actually wronged you and whom you are quietly waiting to see get what they deserve. Do one concrete good toward them this week — pray for them by name, speak well of them, or reach out — chosen precisely because it refuses to let their wrong shape you into someone hard. Taylor mailed a letter of concern to the man who robbed him blind.

fields.title: One Cash Left
fields.body_html:
“The young lions suffer want and hunger; but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.” — Psalm 34:10 (ESV)

By now Taylor had settled in Ningpo and had done something that made the money question far sharper: he had resigned from the society that paid his salary, because it had fallen into debt, and Taylor was convinced from Scripture that he should “owe no man anything.” He would depend on God directly — no salary, no fundraising appeals, no borrowing. Over the mantelpiece in the house he shared with his fellow-worker Mr. Jones, two scrolls hung in Chinese characters: Ebenezer — “Hitherto the Lord has helped us” — and Jehovah-Jireh — “The Lord will provide.” They were about to be tested to the last coin.

The two men were also feeding the poor — sometimes seventy destitute people came for breakfast every day. And the money ran out. It ran out so completely that on the 6th of January 1858 they were down to a single cash between them — a coin worth about a twentieth of a penny. There was enough in the house for one thin breakfast, and after that, nothing: no food, and no money to buy any.

They decided, reluctantly, to sell something. The one thing the Chinese would readily buy was an iron stove they owned, though they hated to part with it. So they set off on foot to the foundry. To get there they needed to cross the river by a floating bridge of boats — but when they arrived, the bridge was gone. It had been swept away during the night. The only way across now was a ferry, and the ferry cost two cash a person. They had one. The road was, quite literally, closed. There was nothing to do but turn around and walk home, and wait for God.

Back at the house they searched the cupboards and found no food — only a small packet of cocoa, which they made with hot water and which somewhat revived them. Mr. Jones had been invited to dine at a friend’s that day, but he refused to go and leave Taylor to go hungry alone. And then the two men got down on their knees together and prayed the plainest prayer there is: give us this day our daily bread. While they were still kneeling, a letter arrived from England. Inside was a remittance of money — enough not only for that day, but for the days after. Taylor’s marriage, as it happened, had already been fixed for exactly fourteen days later. God had cut it that fine, and no finer.

Do not turn this into a promise that God always shows up at the last second with cash. Taylor himself was scrupulously honest that his faith “often, often failed,” that the difficulty was real, and that the hunger that day was real. What the story shows is not that following God is financially safe — it plainly was not — but that God can be depended on right down to the last cash, and that he often lets you get there.

That is the part people miss. Taylor did not have a comfortable margin that made trust easy. He got all the way to one coin, a swept-away bridge, and a cup of cocoa. God did not spare him the emptiness; he met him at the bottom of it. And Taylor came out saying he would not have missed the trial for anything, because it taught him God in a way comfort never could have.

You will probably not be down to a twentieth of a penny. But you will hit real limits — of money, of ability, of options — where you genuinely cannot see how it works out, and where every escape route is a swept-away bridge. The lesson of the cocoa is not that God removes those moments. It is that he is trustworthy inside them, and that the bottom is often exactly where you finally meet him.

One thing to do when you hit a wall you cannot see past: instead of scrambling to manufacture your own escape or quietly panicking, name the need as plainly as Taylor did — “give us this day our daily bread” — and take it to God specifically before you take it anywhere else. He let two grown men get down to one coin and a packet of cocoa, and he did not let them fall.

fields.title: Written in the Margin
fields.body_html:
“Then he said to his disciples, ‘The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.’” — Matthew 9:37–38 (ESV)

Failing health eventually forced Taylor back to England, and he thought it was a disaster. His work in China had never been more fruitful; leaving felt like abandoning it. But those years at home, staring daily at a huge map of China on his study wall, did something the busy years in the field never could. From the field, he had only been able to see the district right around him. From England, he could see the whole vast country — eleven inland provinces with no missionary at all, tens of thousands of people dying every day without ever hearing of Christ. And it began to crush him.

He became convinced that reaching inland China would need a whole new kind of mission. He also became convinced, slowly, that God wanted him to lead it — to ask God for the workers and then go with them. And for a long time he refused. Not because he doubted God would provide the workers or the money; he was sure of that. He refused because he was afraid. If he recruited young, inexperienced Christians and led them into real danger and hardship, some of them might break down — and blame him. So he said nothing, and asked for no one.

But the refusing was its own agony. He put it in stark terms: because he would not ask, the workers did not come; because the workers did not come, people kept dying. He called the feeling “blood-guiltiness,” and it grew until he could not sleep and his health broke down again. A friend invited him to Brighton to rest. And on Sunday the 25th of June, 1865, Taylor sat in a church among a thousand or more comfortable Christians “rejoicing in their own security,” and he could not stand it. He walked out, alone, onto the beach, in what he called great spiritual agony.

There, on the sand, he gave in. He told God that all the responsibility for what happened — every consequence, every risk to every worker — would rest on God, not on him; that his own job was simply to obey and follow, and God’s job was to lead, provide, and protect. And the moment he surrendered it, peace flooded in. Then he did something concrete. He asked God, specifically, for twenty-four fellow workers: two for each of the eleven unreached inland provinces, and two for Mongolia. And he took the Bible he had with him and wrote the request in the margin. A number. A date. In ink.

That prayer on the beach became the China Inland Mission. Within a year, on the 26th of May 1866, Taylor sailed for China again aboard the Lammermuir with a party of missionaries — the beginning of a work that would, over the following decades, put workers across inland China exactly as that pencilled margin had asked.

Look closely at what actually freed him, because it is the opposite of what you would guess. Taylor was not paralysed by weak faith in God; he was sure God would send workers and money. He was paralysed by fear of being blamed — of the responsibility landing on him if it went wrong. What broke the paralysis was handing that responsibility back to God: the outcome is yours, not mine; I only have to obey. That is what let him write a terrifyingly specific request in the margin of his Bible.

You are held back by the same thing more often than you admit. Not usually by doubting God can do something, but by dreading how it will land on you if you step out and it fails. Taylor’s beach is the answer: the results were never yours to carry. Your job is to obey. His job is everything else.

One thing to do: take the step you have been avoiding out of fear of how it might reflect on you, and make it real the way Taylor did — write it down. A specific ask, a date, in a place you will see it. Then hand the outcome to God in as many words: the obeying is mine, the results are yours. That is the exact move that turned a frightened, guilt-ridden man on a beach into the founder of a mission.
